lead: Generative models can act as conditional priors for images. A prior supplies plausible missing content; a condition ties that content to the pixels you already have. For image editing you move in latent space or pass an attribute label. For inpainting you pass a mask and visible pixels. For super-resolution you pass a low-resolution image. The same generator then predicts an edited, filled or upscaled image. Phone galleries, e-commerce catalogue clean-up, medical scan enhancement and CCTV restoration use these tasks.
prereq: You need autoencoders (6.1), VAEs (6.3), GANs (6.4) and autoregressive priors (6.5).

sections.h3: Image editing by moving in latent space

blocks.text: An encoder maps image x to a latent vector z; a decoder maps z back to pixels. If the model is trained well, nearby z values give similar images. An attribute direction d is a vector in latent space. Adding it shifts one property. Common choices are smile, hair colour, age or season. A simple estimate takes the mean encoded vector of images with the attribute minus the mean without it, then normalises to unit length. Large step size changes more but risks artifacts.

blocks.where: z′ is the edited latent code; z is the original latent code; α is the step size in latent units; d is the unit attribute direction.

blocks.text: Conditional GANs and VAEs learn the edit directly. The generator sees a condition c, such as “add glasses”, a sketch, or a reference photo, and samples G(z,c). Paired training data has target images. The loss combines reconstruction, adversarial and sometimes identity losses. CycleGAN handles unpaired style change: two generators map domain A to B and back, and a cycle loss ‖F(G(x)) − x‖₁ keeps content. It is used for photo-to-sketch or summer-to-winter looks.

items: Pick a direction d or a condition c.
Decode z + α d or G(z,c).
Check identity and artifacts; reduce α if needed.

blocks.text: Inpainting fills a hole in an image. The input is a visible image x and a binary mask m. m = 1 marks missing pixels. The model predicts the hole from context: p(y | x ⊙ (1 − m), m), where y is the full target image, x is the observed image, m is a binary mask with m = 1 at missing pixels, and ⊙ is the elementwise product. A context encoder is an encoder-decoder trained to reconstruct the whole image but scored mainly on the hole. The mask is passed as an extra channel so the network knows what to ignore. A plain L1 or L2 loss gives a blurry average fill; a GAN or perceptual decoder adds texture.

items: Make a mask that covers the object or damage.
Feed the masked image and mask channel to the generator.
Composite: output = m ⊙ prediction + (1 − m) ⊙ input.
Train with hole-only pixel loss plus adversarial or perceptual loss.
Evaluate on held-out holes with PSNR/SSIM and human inspection.

blocks.text: Single-image super-resolution maps a low-resolution image to a high-resolution one. A CNN or ResNet predicts missing high-frequency detail; a GAN sharpens texture. Pixel loss alone gives smooth, safe outputs. Perceptual loss compares deep features from a pretrained network and usually looks sharper. SSIM compares local luminance, contrast and structure; it takes values up to 1 (typically between 0 and 1), and equals 1 for identical images. PSNR can rank a blurry result above a sharp one, so report SSIM or a perceptual metric too. Deep image prior is a side note: an untrained network's structure itself favours natural images, so it can denoise or inpaint without training data.

blocks.where: MAX is the maximum pixel value (255 for 8-bit images); MSE is the mean squared error between the output and the target.

blocks.text: The same conditional setup appears in security restoration of CCTV frames. Ethical misuse of restored or edited media belongs to 6.7.

examples.question: A 256×256 8-bit image has a 64×64 masked square. (a) What fraction and percentage of the image is missing? (b) The filled region has MSE = 16 in pixel-level squared error on 8-bit pixels. Compute PSNR. Take MAX = 255.
examples.answer: 6.25% of the image is missing, and the PSNR is 36.09 dB.
examples.check:
import math
H = 256
W = 256
h = 64
w = 64
missing = (h * w) / (H * W)
pct = missing * 100
mse = 16
psnr = 10 * math.log10((255 ** 2) / mse)
print(missing)
print(round(pct, 2))
print(round(psnr, 2))

traps: Higher PSNR does not always mean a better-looking image; PSNR rewards smooth blur. Report SSIM or a perceptual metric as well.
In inpainting, fix the mask polarity: m = 1 means missing, not visible. Composite with m ⊙ prediction + (1 − m) ⊙ input.

Super-resolution input is low-resolution. Evaluate on held-out low/high-resolution pairs, not on training patches, and build the low-resolution training inputs with the same downscaling (degradation) you will meet at test time.
CycleGAN's cycle loss preserves content; adversarial loss alone can change identity. A latent edit's step size α is in latent units, not pixels.

quiz.q: What is the role of the mask in an inpainting model?
quiz.a: It marks which pixels are missing so the generator conditions on the visible context and fills only the hole.

quiz.q: Why can PSNR prefer a blurry super-resolution output over a sharp one?
quiz.a: PSNR depends on MSE. A smooth blur can have low average error, while sharp texture may move pixels and raise MSE even when it looks better.

quiz.q: A 128×128 image has a 32×32 missing square. What fraction and percentage is missing?
For 8-bit pixels, MSE = 25. Compute PSNR with MAX = 255.
In CycleGAN, what stops the generator from mapping every input to one convincing image in the target domain?
quiz.a: The cycle-consistency loss: F(G(x)) must return close to x. The two mappings must be inverses, so content is preserved.

quiz.q: How does a conditional GAN differ from an unconditional GAN for image editing?
quiz.a: The conditional generator also receives c, such as an attribute label or reference image, so it can target a requested change.

quiz.q: A latent edit with large α produces artifacts. What does that suggest about the latent space?
quiz.a: The large step leaves the region where training images are dense, so the decoder sees an unlikely code. Use a smaller α or project back toward the data manifold.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern photo apps use diffusion models for inpainting and super-resolution, but the task setup and metrics here still apply. Search terms: image-to-image translation, context encoder, perceptual loss, LPIPS, Real-ESRGAN, diffusion inpainting. Research often separates distortion metrics (PSNR, SSIM) from perceptual metrics (LPIPS, FID).
